content: {"id": "ed290a03-891b-47c0-98c3-13ca26510b20", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "1434dd1e-eeea-4f15-afc3-fbccb05749ed", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "Application Load Balancer vs Network Load Balancer"}]}

{"id": "7870fd31-8ed8-448a-8cd0-4d7f1070d3bf", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Both are AWS Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) options, but they operate at different layers and are suited to different use cases:

**Application Load Balancer (ALB)**
- Operates at Layer 7 (application layer, HTTP/HTTPS)
- Routes traffic based on content — URL path, hostname, HTTP headers, query strings
- Supports advanced routing: path-based and host-based rules, redirects, fixed responses
- Good for microservices, container-based apps, and anything needing smart HTTP routing
- Supports WebSockets and HTTP/2
- Integrates well with ECS, EKS, Lambda targets

**Network Load Balancer (NLB)**
- Operates at Layer 4 (transport layer, TCP/UDP/TLS)
- Routes based on IP protocol data — much lower latency, built for extreme performance
- Can handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency
- Preserves the client's source IP by default
- Supports static IP addresses / Elastic IPs per Availability Zone — useful when clients need to allowlist fixed IPs
- Good for latency-sensitive workloads, TCP/UDP-based protocols, or when you need a static IP

**Quick rule of thumb:** if you need smart HTTP-level routing (paths, hosts, headers), go with ALB. If you need raw performance, static IPs, or non-HTTP protocols (like TCP/UDP), go with NLB.

Let me know if you want help figuring out which one fits a specific setup you're working with, or want to see your existing load balancers.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
